item.title: Commentary: China's space station opens a new chapter in int'l cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
Commentary: China's space station opens a new chapter in int'l cooperation This undated photo shows Shenzhou-24 crew members Tang Hongbo (C), Wu Yi (R), and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali. (Xinhua) BEIJING, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- The Shenzhou-24 mission marks a milestone in China's manned space program as a Pakistani astronaut becomes the first foreign astronaut to board China's Tiangong space station, opening a new chapter in China's efforts to advance international cooperation in space exploration. Over the years, China has built its space station through independent innovation and technological development, demonstrating its growing capabilities in manned spaceflight. Its experience shows that self-reliance and international cooperation are not mutually exclusive. While independent development has laid a solid foundation for China's space program, openness is creating new opportunities for its continued progress. China has increasingly sought to make its space program more accessible to international partners, offering opportunities for other countries to participate in scientific research and space exploration. The Shenzhou-24 mission is a concrete step in this direction. For Pakistan, the mission offers an opportunity to develop expertise in human spaceflight, strengthen its astronaut training capabilities and participate in scientific experiments in orbit. For China, it marks the first joint spaceflight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts, extending bilateral cooperation into a new frontier. The experience could also pave the way for broader international participation in China's space program. Space exploration transcends national borders and offers opportunities for countries to advance scientific knowledge through cooperation. China has consistently advocated the peaceful use of outer space and promoted international collaboration in this field. A case in point is China's recent donation to the United Nations of a lunar soil sample collected by the Chang'e-6 mission from the far side of the Moon. By sharing the fruits of its space exploration with the international community, China is helping create opportunities for joint research and enabling more countries to benefit from advances in space science. This photo taken on Sept. 14, 2026 shows a lunar sample collected from the far side of the Moon by China's Chang'e-6 mission, in Vienna, Austria. (Xinhua/He Canling) Space exploration should not be an exclusive endeavor, but a shared undertaking that brings countries together through the exchange of knowledge, technology and talent. By opening its space station to international partners, China is creating opportunities for scientific collaboration and contributing to the peaceful use of outer space. item.title: China launches Shenzhou-24 spaceship to Tiangong space station with first foreign astronaut on board
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
China launches Shenzhou-24 spaceship to Tiangong space station with first foreign astronaut on board The Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship, atop a Long March-2F carrier rocket, blasts off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, Nov. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Minggang) JIUQUAN, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- China launched the Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship on Wednesday, sending three astronauts, including a Pakistani payload specialist, to its orbiting Tiangong space station. The spaceship, atop a Long March-2F carrier rocket, blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China. The astronauts aboard the spaceship are mission commander and spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi, and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first-ever foreign astronaut to visit Tiangong. The Shenzhou-24 mission marks the first joint flight consisting of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program. During the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, seven AlphaBot robots stationed at the media center provided services for Chinese and foreign journalists, operating reliably and serving drinks over seven consecutive days. These robots are from Ai² Robotics, a robotics startup founded in early 2023 in Shenzhen by Guo Yandong. Guo believes that humanoid robots must be deployed in real scenarios for practical assignments. With this end goal in mind, he has oriented Ai² Robotics toward developing productivity-focused intelligent robots. The AlphaBot robots are now in service across Shenzhen for airport, industrial, urban governance and emergency-response tasks. Guo's vision of robots as the fourth-generation intelligent terminals following personal computers, mobile phones and smart vehicles is steadily taking shape. item.title: Send-off ceremony held for Shenzhou-24 astronauts
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
Send-off ceremony held for Shenzhou-24 astronauts A send-off ceremony for the Shenzhou-24 crew, consisting of two Chinese astronauts and one Pakistani astronaut, is held at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, Nov. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Lian Zhen) JIUQUAN, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- A send-off ceremony for the Shenzhou-24 crew, consisting of two Chinese astronauts and one Pakistani astronaut, was held early Wednesday morning at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi, and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali set off at 5:28 a.m. (Beijing Time). To date, the Shenzhou-23 astronauts have stayed in the orbiting Tiangong space station for more than 180 days. They are in good physical and mental condition and are actively preparing to welcome the arrival of the three Shenzhou-24 astronauts, according to the CMSA. The Shenzhou-24 spaceship is slated to be launched at 8:18 a.m. (Beijing Time) on Wednesday, the agency noted. item.title: Xi Story: Vision over a century old meets a changing China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
Xi Story: Vision over a century old meets a changing China BEIJING, Nov. 24 (Xinhua) -- Dr. Sun Yat-sen once envisioned an ambitious blueprint for China's modernization in a landmark work compiled from his writings finished between 1917 and 1919, featuring plans for an extensive railway and road network as well as world-class ports. "Many of the goals Dr. Sun Yat-sen set forth have been realized, and what we have accomplished has gone far beyond anything he could have imagined," President Xi Jinping said last week at a museum in honor of Sun, one of the nation's revered revolutionary forefathers, in south China's Guangdong Province. This year marks the 160th anniversary of Sun's birth. Upon arrival at the museum located in the city of Zhongshan, Sun's hometown, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, laid a floral basket before the pioneer's bronze statue and bowed in tribute. Born in 1866, Sun led the Revolution of 1911 more than a century ago to abolish the absolute monarchy that had ruled China for thousands of years. Earlier in November, Xi addressed a gathering held in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing to mark Sun's 160th birth anniversary, hailing Sun as "a great national hero, a great patriot, and a great pioneer of China's democratic revolution." At the gathering, Xi highlighted Sun's lifelong devotion to the country, noting that Sun's call for "revitalizing China" has inspired generation after generation of Chinese, taking on renewed significance with each passing era. The president called for carrying forward Sun's legacy, working together to advance national rejuvenation, and turning into reality the great dream of all Chinese people since the advent of modern times. Xi's visit to the museum, part of an inspection tour in Zhongshan on Nov. 16, offered a glimpse of how Sun's vision of a strong and prosperous China has taken shape today. Sun once envisioned developing the country around three great ports -- in the north, the east and the south. The three powerhouses of China's economy today, the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, the Yangtze River Delta and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, echo Sun's original design, Xi noted at the museum. "Dr. Sun's national railway map envisaged 160,000 kilometers," Xi said, noting that China's railway network has since surpassed that figure. By the end of 2025, the country's railway network had spanned 165,000 kilometers in total, including 50,000 kilometers of operational high-speed railway, which accounted for 70 percent of the world's total. "Today, the Chinese economy ranks second in the world. Chinese people have achieved moderate prosperity in all respects, and the Chinese nation has stood up, grown rich and become strong," Xi said. China is also continuing to make new contributions to the development and progress of human society, he added. This transformation Sun once dreamed of is also evident in his hometown and the surrounding area. Before visiting the museum, Xi inspected the Shenzhen-Zhongshan Link, a mega cross-sea passage connecting cities on opposite sides of the Pearl River Estuary. The link cuts travel time between the technology hub of Shenzhen and the manufacturing city of Zhongshan from about two hours to roughly 30 minutes, facilitating integration across the Greater Bay Area. Over the years, Xi has made several inspection tours of the Greater Bay Area. Sun's former residence and the museum exhibition hall in Zhongshan are just a short distance apart. "I have been here before, but this visit has given me new impressions," Xi said. "The great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation has entered an irreversible historical process," Xi said, calling for sustained efforts to advance the great cause. item.title: Power use surges in China's EV charging, data service sectors in October
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
Power use surges in China's EV charging, data service sectors in October BEIJING, Nov. 23 (Xinhua) -- Electricity consumption by China's electric vehicle charging and internet data service sectors soared in October, highlighting robust demand from the country's fast-growing new-energy vehicle and digital industries, official data showed Monday. Power consumption by charging and battery-swapping services reached 18.6 billion kilowatt-hours in October, surging 59.4 percent year on year, while that of internet data services jumped 34.7 percent to 9.9 billion kilowatt-hours, according to the National Energy Administration. NEVs accounted for 64.3 percent of new car sales last month, up from 61.6 percent in September, while the cumulative share for the first 10 months climbed to 54.8 percent, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. China's total electricity consumption for October stood at 870.9 billion kilowatt-hours, an increase of 1.6 percent year on year. Driven by rapid growth in electricity consumption by new business forms, power use in the tertiary industry grew the fastest among all industries, said Wu Liqiang, an official with the China Electricity Council. Electricity consumption by the tertiary industry rose 6.3 percent year on year to 171.4 billion kilowatt-hours in October. Electricity consumption by the primary industry stood at 12.4 billion kilowatt-hours, up 3.3 percent year on year, while power use by the secondary industry edged up 1.8 percent to 579 billion kilowatt-hours. Notably, power consumption by high-tech and equipment manufacturing industries climbed 6.5 percent year on year to 111.1 billion kilowatt-hours in October. In October, power use in high energy-consuming manufacturing sector posted negative year-on-year growth for three consecutive months, said Wu. In the first 10 months of 2026, China's total electricity consumption rose 3.7 percent year on year to 8.94 trillion kilowatt-hours. Electricity use by charging and battery-swapping services surged 55.9 percent in this period, while that of internet data services increased by 40.8 percent. According to an annual development report on China's electric power industry released by the China Electricity Council in July, total electricity consumption nationwide in 2026 is expected to increase by 5 percent to 6 percent year on year. item.title: Why is Europe's tech spotlight brightening with Chinese innovations?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
Why is Europe's tech spotlight brightening with Chinese innovations? Chinese humanoid robots perform at Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. (Photo/websummit.com) At Web Summit 2026 recently held in Lisbon, Portugal, performances by humanoid robots from China stole the spotlight. Clips quickly gained traction on social media, giving overseas netizens a closer look at the appeal of Chinese technology. At the opening ceremony, Web Summit CEO and founder Paddy Cosgrave said that future technology superstars would increasingly come from China. At a premier global tech gathering hosted in Europe, why did Chinese tech elements keep standing out, and why was China's presence growing more prominent? China's strong innovation capabilities are the most direct explanation. Chinese companies including Tencent, Xiaomi, Unitree Robotics, and Pony.ai, participated in this year's summit, showcasing breakthroughs across frontier fields such as artificial intelligence (AI), embodied AI, and autonomous driving. At the event, which brought together roughly 70,000 technology professionals, entrepreneurs and investors from around the world, Chinese innovations captured the attention of global industry players, thanks to solid technological foundations and competitive products. The growing attention to Chinese innovation also reflects a subtle shift in the global innovation landscape. This year's opening ceremony featured a dedicated frontier technology showcase. Chinese companies were invited to present solutions such as humanoid robots and flying cars, painting a picture of everyday life in the future for European audiences. Staff members collect data in a range of scenarios at an embodied AI robot data collection and training center in Suqian, east China's Jiangsu province. (Photo/Wang Shuaifu) For years, Silicon Valley and Europe's established research hubs were synonymous with global innovation centers. Today, when Europe looks for a tangible glimpse of tomorrow, its gaze is turning proactively toward China. That marks a shift in how the international community views China's role in innovation. Looking deeper, the rising prominence of Chinese innovations in Europe reflects not only shared needs, but also the inevitable logic of industrial development. Europe is home to many top universities and long-standing prowess in basic research and high-end manufacturing, yet faces bottlenecks in commercializing innovation. These include an underdeveloped digital platform ecosystem, limited cloud computing capacity, and slower AI commercialization. Bridging the "last mile" from lab breakthroughs to market application remains a persistent challenge for European industry. China's innovation drive has charted a differentiated path. By leveraging a massive engineering workforce, a complete industrial chain, and vast application scenarios, new technologies can rapidly complete a closed-loop iteration from laboratory to production line to real-world applications. Robots do more than perform on stage. They help in warehouses and retail stores. AI goes beyond conversations. It cuts costs and raises efficiency in industrial settings. What truly resonates in Europe is the substantial application potential and win-win business opportunities behind these innovations. Still, discordant voices persist. Even as growing numbers of business leaders and researchers recognize China as an indispensable force on the global innovation landscape, some European politicians remain conflicted about Chinese technology. They repeatedly hype the "de-risking" narrative and erect barriers in an attempt to restrict China-Europe cooperation on the sci-tech front. Yet such moves have neither changed the stance of the business and tech communities nor halted the endogenous drive for bilateral cooperation. Sci-tech cooperation between China and Europe is inherently built on complementary strengths. Europe's basic research and talent pool complement China's engineering capabilities and application testing. They are closely aligned in such fields as AI, green technology, and smart manufacturing. Foreign visitors watch a performance by a humanoid robot and a quadruped robot dog at a direct-operated store of Unitree Robotics on Wangfujing pedestrian street in Beijing. (Photo/Guo Junfeng) European enterprises can draw on Chinese solutions to accelerate digital transformation, while Chinese innovation entities can leverage European resources to enhance their technologies. This model of mutual empowerment has a solid foundation and enjoys broad room to grow. Sci-tech innovation is not a zero-sum game, and pursuing technological self-reliance is by no means synonymous with self-isolation. Choosing diverse technology supply and broad collaborative networks gives industrial development greater resilience. Equating competition with a threat or dismissing pragmatic cooperation as dependence only limits oneself and hinders future growth. When Europe's tech community looks toward China, it sees not only today's technological achievements, but a future of cooperation. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Experts warn against protectionism, call for pragmatic China-EU engagement
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
Experts warn against protectionism, call for pragmatic China-EU engagement BELGRADE, Nov. 24 (Xinhua) -- European and Chinese experts on Monday called for a more pragmatic approach to China-Europe relations and stronger multilateral cooperation, warning that trade protectionism could hurt European consumers and undermine investment. The remarks were made at a panel discussion on the future of China-Europe relations hosted by the Belgrade-based Center for International Relations and Sustainable Development (CIRSD). Under the theme "De-Risking the Win-Win? The Trillion-Euro Question," the discussion explored how China and Europe could maintain mutually beneficial economic cooperation amid growing trade tensions and geopolitical uncertainties. Discussing recent trade arrangements between China and the EU concerning hybrid vehicles, Rudiger Frank, professor of East Asian economy and society at the University of Vienna, warned of the broader economic consequences of trade restrictions. He said artificially higher consumer prices could fuel inflation, push up interest rates, increase borrowing costs and discourage investment, creating a "vicious cycle" for the European economy. Frank advocated a multilateral approach to addressing trade imbalances, citing the WTO as an existing institutional framework and arguing that countries should seek an overall trade balance rather than balanced trade with each individual partner. Zhou Bo, a senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, called on both China and Europe to set aside prejudices, adopt a realistic and pragmatic approach, and seek common ground for cooperation. Vuk Jeremic, president of CIRSD and former president of the United Nations General Assembly, who moderated the discussion, said closer cooperation with China could contribute to Europe's efforts to achieve strategic autonomy and economic prosperity. Jeremic said Europe needs to increase productivity and regain competitiveness, goals that could be advanced through closer, albeit careful, engagement with China rather than isolating itself from a major global economy and industrial and technological powerhouse. He said Europe should find ways to leverage its already substantial economic ties with China, addressing risks where necessary without sacrificing the potential of bilateral cooperation. item.title: China's investment in new-type power grids expected to exceed 5 trillion yuan: What makes them different?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
China's investment in new-type power grids expected to exceed 5 trillion yuan: What makes them different? China has built the world's largest power supply system. In the first nine months of this year, the country's total electricity consumption surpassed 8.07 trillion kilowatt-hours, up 3.9 percent year on year. Meanwhile, China's power system is undergoing a series of changes on both the supply and demand sides. New energy is playing an increasingly prominent role in China's power mix, but it also brings greater volatility and uncertainty to the power grid. At the same time, the continued growth of emerging industries is creating higher demands for power quality. Photo shows a photovoltaic power station on Tunbashan Mountain in Mengshan county, Wuzhou, south China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. (Photo/Wu Guangsheng) A meeting of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee held on April 28, 2026, called for efforts to step up the planning and construction of water networks, new-type power grids, computing infrastructure, new-generation communications networks, urban underground pipelines, and logistics systems. The development of new-type power grids has thus been incorporated into the country's top-level design. A robust power grid is essential to ensuring an adequate, safe, and reliable electricity supply. How is China advancing the rollout of these systems? "Compared with traditional power grids, building new-type power grids demands greater systems thinking. It should be rooted in regional resource endowments, industrial structures, load characteristics and distribution, while coordinating planning with the territorial spatial layout across time and space. This will enable the optimal allocation of energy resources across regions on a larger scale," said Yan Xiaoqing, director of the energy strategy research office of the energy institute under the State Grid Energy Research Institute Co., Ltd. A power grid consists of a backbone transmission network, distribution networks and smart microgrids, much like a three-tier road network of expressways, urban and rural roads, and neighborhood streets, Yan explained. The key to developing new-type power grids is to optimize this new grid architecture, Yan said, noting that the effective coordination among the main grid, distribution networks and microgrids levels provides reliable electricity support for the energy transition and high-quality development. "During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), investment in China's new-type power grids is expected to exceed 5 trillion yuan (about $749.87 billion). 15 additional ultra-high-voltage direct-current (UHVDC) transmission links are expected to be commissioned. Efforts will also be made to upgrade distribution networks through digital and intelligent technologies and accelerate the development of smart microgrids," said Yang Zhengang, senior manager of the planning management division of China Southern Power Grid's planning department. If the new architecture provides the framework, new technologies serve as its supporting tools. New energy storage systems: A "stabilizer" for power grids Photo shows an energy storage project in Pinglu county, Yuncheng, north China's Shanxi province. (Photo/Quan Yongjun) In Huangjiabu township, Yuyao, Ningbo, east China's Zhejiang province, 49 white energy storage containers stand in rows across the site of a 50-megawatt/100-megawatt-hour independent energy storage power station operated by a new energy company based in Ningbo. Inside the containers, different battery technologies serve distinct purposes. Lithium iron phosphate batteries on the eastern side offer large storage capacity and are used for peak shaving and valley filling, while lithium titanate batteries in the northwest respond more rapidly and are designed to address fluctuations in grid frequency. When the grid experiences fluctuations, the latter can adjust their power output within tens of milliseconds, compared with about 30 seconds for conventional thermal power units. Ningbo was the first city in China to surpass 10 million kilowatts of installed distributed photovoltaic (PV) capacity. But PV power generation depends on weather conditions: even a passing cloud can cause sharp fluctuations in output. From peak shaving and valley filling to rapid power response, new energy storage systems help ensure that fluctuating green electricity can not only be generated but also used reliably. They effectively serve as a readily available "power bank" and "stabilizer" for the urban grid. Artificial intelligence: Turning fluctuations into predictability This year, the summer peak in electricity consumption arrived more than a month earlier than usual. In late May, "Tianxiang," an artificial intelligence (AI) large model developed by China Southern Power Grid for meteorological forecasting, accurately identified the extreme heat expected in the second half of the month a week in advance. Another AI-powered load forecasting agent, "Tianyan," predicted electricity demand under high-temperature conditions 14 days ahead. It identified the prospect of high evening peak loads in south China's Guangdong province and a sharp decline in renewable energy output in southwest China's Yunnan province, helping power dispatch authorities prepare for the challenges posed by extreme heat. From forecasting and simulation to planning and inspection, AI is increasingly being integrated into every aspect of power grid operations. AI represents one of the most important technological directions for new-type power grids, said Xiao Liang, a technical expert at the dispatching and control center of China Southern Power Grid. AI helps optimize the allocation of grid resources and ensure the security of electricity supply, according to Xiao. New services: Making power supply more flexible A robotic dog conducts an inspection at a substation in Daxi township, Wenling, east China's Zhejiang province. (Photo/Xu Weijie) Ultimately, upgrades to grid architecture and technology are aimed at improving services. In Shenzhen, a "power plant" without a physical facility -- a virtual power plant -- is providing a new form of electricity service to the city. "As a new model in the power sector, the virtual power plant creates a pool of resources that can be flexibly coordinated. It brings together distributed and adjustable resources, including charging piles, building air-conditioning systems, and distributed energy storage facilities, and deeply integrates them with AI technologies to participate in power grid regulation," said Li Jiangnan, senior manager of the virtual power plant's management center. The center's management platform has connected 61 operators and more than 14,000 users, aggregating over 1.4 million kilowatts of real-time adjustable load capacity, equivalent to that of a medium-sized coal-fired power plant, Li said. The development of new-type power grids represents a profound transformation in grid architecture, technologies, and services, requiring coordinated planning and systematic measures. Tan Hongjiang, deputy director of the electricity department of China's National Energy Administration, said the administration would continue to advance the development of new-type power grids by optimizing new grid architecture, making breakthroughs in key new technologies, upgrading new power grid services, and stepping up efforts to advance the implementation of major tasks and projects.
